query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys processed by additive manufacturing, employing a slower cooling rate after solution treatment will promote the coarsening of gamma' nano‐precipitates. These larger precipitates will more effectively pin mobile grain boundaries through a Zener drag effect, resulting in a serrated grain boundary morphology that distributes strain more uniformly. This structural change retards intergranular crack propagation and retains toughness (i.e., improved tensile fracture strain and extended creep rupture life) compared to alloys rapidly quenched to retain a fine, homogeneous precipitate distribution.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy (e.g., with an L12 gamma' precipitate phase) processed by selective laser melting and subjected to a standard solution treatment followed by a rapid quench that results in a straight (non-serrated) grain boundary morphology.
generation.intervention: Vary the post‐solution treatment cooling rate by employing a controlled slow cooling (e.g., 1°C/min) versus a rapid water quench.
generation.conditions: Tensile and creep tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 650°C) on alloys with comparable composition and initial microstructure, processed by SLM followed by the prescribed heat treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: Coarsened gamma' precipitates that interact with migrating grain boundaries to produce a serrated morphology.
generation.mechanism: The coarsened gamma' precipitates exert a Zener drag on moving grain boundaries during slow cooling, causing them to become serrated. This serrated morphology reduces local strain concentrations at triple junctions and hinders intergranular crack propagation, thereby increasing the alloy's toughness under high-temperature service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (rapidly quenched samples with straight grain boundaries), the slow-cooled samples will exhibit serrated grain boundaries, a more uniform strain distribution, and measurable improvements in tensile fracture strain (potentially by a factor similar to literature observations) as well as increased creep rupture life.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples that have been solution-treated and then rapidly quenched, resulting in a fine, homogeneous nano-precipitate distribution and straight grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold in high-entropy alloy systems processed by SLM with an L12 type gamma' precipitate phase, demonstrated under elevated temperature loading (e.g., ~650°C). Its validity may be limited if other significant microstructural features (e.g., secondary phases, extreme processing defects) dominate the fracture behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of toughness improvement is uncertain and may depend on additional factors such as alloy composition, detailed precipitate size distribution, and precise thermal profiles beyond the simple cooling rate change.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples using selective laser melting. Subject both sets to the same solution treatment but apply different cooling protocols: one set is rapidly water quenched (baseline) and the other is slowly cooled (e.g., 1°C/min) to encourage precipitate coarsening. Characterize the grain boundary morphology via SEM to confirm serration in the slow-cooled samples. Then conduct tensile and creep tests at around 650°C to compare fracture strain and rupture life between the two sets.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology (e.g., serration vs. straight) via SEM/TEM imaging
Precipitate size distribution via microstructural analysis
Tensile fracture strain at elevated temperature (650°C)
Creep rupture life under standardized loading conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not show significantly coarser precipitates with corresponding serrated grain boundaries, or if there is no measurable improvement in tensile fracture strain and/or creep rupture life relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, then the hypothesis that precipitate-induced serration governs toughness retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To study the interactions between precipitates and grain boundary morphology, interrupted cooling experiment was conducted, and microstructure evolution was captured during slow cooling to various temperatures (Figure 4). After solution treatment for 1 h at 1120°C followed by water quenching, no precipitates could be observed (Figure 4(a)). With 1°C/min slow cooling to 1060°C, homogeneous distribution of spherical precipitates could be seen, and a slight distortion of grain boundary was observed (Figure 4(b)). With further cooling to 1000°C, blocky and floral precipitate could be identified, and serrations of grain boundary were clearly identified (Figure 4(c)).

This work has demonstrated that a simple post heat treatment could induce SEGB in a HEA fabricated by SLM. The serrations on grain boundary in HT-samples were attributed to the blocky irregular shaped γ′ precipitates formed during the slow cooling process, and they could pin the mobile grain boundaries as well as restricting grain growth, this phenomenon is known as the Zener drag effect []. The drag force from the coarse precipitates would hinder the migration of grain boundary, while those free from the precipitates could break free around the precipitates and resulted in serrated morphology (Figure 4(c)). The inhibition of grain growth from coarse precipitates explained why HT-2 sample possessed a smaller grain size than that of HT-1 sample. The difference in tensile yield strength between HT-1 and HT-2 at 25°C and 650°C could be associated with the size of γ′ precipitates. According to Jackson – Reed model [], the strengthening contribution of γ′ precipitate could be inverse proportional to the average radius of the precipitate. The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.
